title: Optimization objectives, constraints and convergence
outcome: Use a prepared optimization library while checking the objective, feasible set and independent convergence evidence.
key_terms: A quasi-Newton method that builds an approximate inverse Hessian from successive gradients to choose search directions.
A function supplied to the optimizer that returns the objective's gradient and should be checked against an independent derivative.
Searching only within stated limits, such as the interval 0 through 2, where the answer may lie on a boundary.
The `Optim.converged` result reports that a stopping criterion was met, not that the global minimum was proven.
approach: Check the problem before the solver. `objective(x) = (x[1]-1)^2 + 4(x[2]+2)^2` is a convex quadratic with minimum 0 at `[1, -2]`. Worked example A runs BFGS with a ForwardDiff gradient, and worked example B minimizes `(x-3)^2` over the interval from 0 to 2. Convergence evidence combines the point, objective value and gradient norm.

exercises.title: Check the objective sign
exercises.task: Replace a minimization objective with its negative.
exercises.hint: State whether the goal is minimization or maximization.
exercises.answer: Successful numerical progress cannot validate a mistaken objective definition.
exercises.why: Negating the quadratic makes it unbounded below, so a minimizer moves away from `[1, -2]` without end.
exercises.wrong: Flipping the sign to turn a maximization into minimization and forgetting to flip it back optimizes the opposite goal.
exercises.verify: Evaluate `-objective` at points farther from `[1, -2]` and confirm it keeps decreasing.

exercises.title: Verify the known optimum
exercises.answer: The test supports this convex fixture rather than a blanket global-convergence claim.
exercises.why: At `[1, -2]` both squared terms are zero, so the objective is 0 and its gradient `[2(x1-1), 8(x2+2)]` is zero.
exercises.wrong: Trusting only the solver's returned point skips an independent check that this point is actually optimal.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `objective([1.0, -2.0]) == 0`, a zero gradient there, and values 1 and 4 at nearby points.

exercises.title: Inspect the feasible set
exercises.task: Minimize the scalar case only on the interval from 0 to 2.
exercises.expected: The best feasible point is near 2.
exercises.answer: Constraints are part of the problem, not an optional display filter.
exercises.why: `(x-3)^2` decreases on the interval from 0 to 2, so the bounded minimizer is the endpoint 2, with value 1.
exercises.wrong: Solving without bounds and then clamping 3 to 2 happens to work here but fails for objectives whose clamped point is not optimal.
exercises.verify: Example B asserts `abs(point-2) < 1e-5` and a minimum near 1; the reference checks `(x-0.5)^2` gives 0.5 inside the interval.

exercises.title: Read convergence evidence
exercises.task: Inspect the returned point, objective and gradient norm.
exercises.expected: They agree with the known quadratic solution.
exercises.hint: A status flag is only one diagnostic.
exercises.answer: Independent mathematical checks make the optimization result more interpretable.
exercises.why: Example A checks `point ≈ [1, -2]`, `Optim.minimum(result) < 1e-12`, a gradient norm below 1e-6 and `Optim.converged(result)`.
exercises.wrong: Reading only the converged flag accepts a run that stopped by a tolerance on a wrong objective or a poor starting point.
exercises.verify: Print the point, objective and `norm(ForwardDiff.gradient(objective, point))` together.

exercises.title: Scale a parameter
exercises.task: Change a parameter unit in a real objective.
exercises.hint: A numeric rescaling can change the scientific specification.
exercises.answer: Conditioning improvements should retain the original interpretation and feasible decisions.
exercises.why: If `x[2]` is changed from meters to centimeters, the weight 4 and the offset 2 must change with it to describe the same problem.
exercises.wrong: Rescaling a parameter for faster convergence but leaving the penalty and bounds in the old units solves a different problem.
exercises.verify: Map the rescaled optimum back to original units and confirm it equals `[1, -2]`.

exercises.title: Assess a fitted model
exercises.task: Observe a lower training objective after optimization.
exercises.expected: Evaluate the frozen procedure on independent data.
exercises.hint: Optimization and generalization are different questions.
exercises.answer: A better fit can still reflect overfitting, leakage or a poor target.
exercises.why: A lower training objective only shows that the optimizer fit these data better, not that predictions improve elsewhere.
exercises.wrong: Reporting the drop in training loss as evidence of model quality ignores overfitting and leakage.
exercises.verify: Freeze the fitted procedure and evaluate it on held-out data, as lesson julia-021 does with its final rows.
